questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy eats a large chocolate-dipped ice cream cone. Within several minutes his plasma insulin concentration rises sharply. Entry of glucose into the pancreatic beta cell, the step that initiates this secretory response, is mediated by which of the following transporters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GLUT1

choices.label: B
choices.text: GLUT2

choices.label: C
choices.text: GLUT3

choices.label: D
choices.text: GLUT4

choices.label: E
choices.text: GLUT5

explanation.summary: Beta cells sense hyperglycemia through insulin-independent GLUT2, the first step in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLUT2 sits in pancreatic beta islet cells (and hepatocytes) and is insulin-independent, so it lets intracellular glucose track serum glucose. Glucose entering through GLUT2 undergoes glycolysis, raising the ATP-to-ADP ratio, closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, depolarizing the cell, and admitting calcium that triggers exocytosis of insulin granules. This is why plasma insulin climbs within about 5 minutes of a glucose load.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 serves most cells, particularly red blood cells and brain, providing basal uptake rather than beta-cell glucose sensing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT3 is expressed in brain and placenta and has no role in triggering insulin release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent transporter of skeletal and cardiac muscle and adipose tissue; it acts downstream of insulin, not upstream of its secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 is a fructose transporter in small intestine, muscle, and testes and does not mediate glucose sensing.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 29-year-old hospital nurse is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed episode of confusion and diaphoresis. Fingerstick glucose is 38 mg/dL. Serum insulin is markedly elevated, C-peptide is undetectable, and a sulfonylurea screen is negative. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin-secreting tumor of pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucagon-secreting tumor of pancreatic alpha cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surreptitious injection of exogenous insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatostatin excess secreted by islet delta cells

explanation.summary: C-peptide separates endogenous hyperinsulinemia from injected insulin, because only proinsulin-derived insulin carries C-peptide with it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta cells cleave proinsulin into mature insulin plus a 31-amino acid C-peptide and release the two into blood in equimolar amounts. Synthetic insulin preparations contain no C-peptide, so injected insulin drives hypoglycemia with high measured insulin and a suppressed or undetectable C-peptide level. That is exactly the pattern here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An insulinoma hypersecretes endogenous insulin, so C-peptide would be elevated in parallel with insulin, not undetectable.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-cell tumors secrete glucagon and cause hyperglycemia with weight loss, diarrhea, and a migratory rash, not hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune beta-cell loss causes insulin deficiency and hyperglycemia; both insulin and C-peptide would be low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin inhibits insulin secretion, so an excess would lower, not raise, the measured insulin level.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus receives a subcutaneous dose of insulin for polyuria and polydipsia. Insulin exerts its effects on target cells by binding to which of the following types of receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G protein-coupled receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ligand-gated ion channel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracellular nuclear hormone receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: JAK-STAT-associated cytokine receptor

explanation.summary: Insulin signals through a receptor tyrosine kinase that also binds IGF-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin binds the insulin receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase that likewise binds insulin-like growth factor 1. Autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues launches the cascade that ends with GLUT4 translocation to the membrane and glucose entry by facilitated diffusion. A separate arm, the MAP kinase pathway, drives cell growth and DNA synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The G protein-coupled receptor with adenylate cyclase and cAMP belongs to glucagon signaling in the liver, not to insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin does not gate an ion channel; the ATP-sensitive potassium channel it is often confused with lies in the beta cell and is not an insulin receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin is a water-soluble peptide that travels unbound in plasma and cannot cross the membrane to reach an intracellular receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: JAK-STAT signaling is implicated in neoplastic and immune disorders but not in insulin action.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has not eaten for 18 hours. Glucagon binds its G protein-coupled receptor on hepatocytes, activating adenylate cyclase and raising intracellular cyclic AMP. This second messenger most directly activates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenylate cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycogen synthase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphoinositide-3-kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitogen-activated protein kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protein kinase A

explanation.summary: In the hepatic glucagon cascade, cAMP activates protein kinase A, which ultimately turns on glycogen phosphorylase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucagon receptor occupancy activates adenylate cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP. cAMP then activates protein kinase A, which activates phosphorylase kinase; that enzyme phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b to the active phosphorylase a, releasing glucose 1-phosphate from glycogen. Glycogenolysis proceeds quickly enough to raise blood sugar within minutes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylate cyclase lies upstream: the G protein activates it, and it generates cAMP rather than being activated by cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen synthase builds glycogen and is favored by insulin in the fed state, the opposite of what glucagon accomplishes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The phosphoinositide-3-kinase arm belongs to insulin receptor signaling and mediates GLUT4 insertion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MAP kinase is the growth and DNA-synthesis arm activated by insulin receptor binding, not by cAMP from glucagon.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman feels dizzy and shaky several hours after skipping lunch. Her home glucometer reads 50 mg/dL. As her pancreatic islets respond to this blood glucose level, which of the following changes in hormone secretion is most likely occurring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased glucagon secretion with increased insulin secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased glucagon secretion with decreased insulin secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased glucagon secretion with decreased insulin secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased glucagon secretion with increased insulin secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased somatostatin secretion with increased insulin secretion

explanation.summary: Alpha and beta cells read the same glucose signal in opposite directions, so hypoglycemia raises glucagon while suppressing insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: At low glucose, alpha cells depolarize, calcium enters through voltage-gated channels, and glucagon granules undergo exocytosis. The beta cell responds to glucose in the opposite direction, so its secretion falls as glucose falls. The result is coordinated counterregulation that mobilizes hepatic glycogen and restores serum glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses both hormones; low glucose stimulates glucagon and suppresses insulin, not the other way around.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucagon direction is wrong: hypoglycemia is the principal stimulus for alpha-cell secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin direction is wrong: insulin release is suppressed, not stimulated, as glucose falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin inhibits islet secretion and would not be paired with a rise in insulin during hypoglycemia.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus forgets his morning insulin dose. His fingerstick glucose is 240 mg/dL, and after 45 minutes of basketball it falls to 150 mg/dL without any insulin having been given. Which of the following best explains the fall in his blood glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contracting skeletal muscle translocates GLUT4 by an insulin-independent pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exercise upregulates hepatic GLUT2, increasing net hepatic glucose uptake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exercise-induced incretin release stimulates residual beta cells to secrete insulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sympathetic activation during exercise suppresses alpha-cell glucagon secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Muscle contraction increases insulin receptor autophosphorylation in myocytes

explanation.summary: Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 to the membrane through a pathway that does not require insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin normally drives GLUT4 translocation in skeletal and cardiac muscle and adipose tissue, but skeletal muscle contraction recruits GLUT4 through a separate, insulin-independent route. That is why exercise lowers glucose even when insulin signaling is absent or impaired, as in this patient who took no insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT2 in hepatocytes is insulin-independent and mediates bidirectional hepatic glucose movement; exercise does not lower systemic glucose by increasing hepatic uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incretins such as GLP-1 and GIP are released after food ingestion, not by exercise, and act on beta cells this patient largely lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic activity during exercise stimulates glucagon release and inhibits insulin, which would tend to raise glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Contraction bypasses the insulin receptor entirely; with no circulating insulin, receptor autophosphorylation cannot account for the drop.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A healthy volunteer drinks 75 g of glucose on one study day and, on another, receives an intravenous glucose infusion producing an identical plasma glucose curve. The insulin rise is substantially greater after the oral load. Which pair of gut-derived incretins most directly accounts for this difference by activating pancreatic beta cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cholecystokinin and secretin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Somatostatin and gastrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucagon and cortisol

choices.label: D
choices.text: GLP-1 and GIP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin and C-peptide

explanation.summary: GLP-1 and GIP are the incretins that amplify beta-cell insulin release when glucose arrives through the gut.
explanation.whyCorrect: Food entering the gut triggers an anticipatory release of insulin mediated by gut hormones. Of these, glucagon-like peptide-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide are specifically the incretins, and they activate pancreatic beta cells in response to elevated glucose. Because intravenous glucose bypasses the gut, no incretin signal is generated and the insulin response is smaller.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholecystokinin and secretin are gut hormones involved in the meal response but are not the incretins that directly activate beta cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Somatostatin inhibits insulin secretion, and gastrin is not an incretin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucagon and cortisol raise blood glucose rather than amplifying insulin release after an oral load.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin and C-peptide are the beta-cell secretory products themselves, not the gut signals that stimulate them.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a hemoglobin A1c of 8.4% is started on liraglutide. Which of the following best describes how this drug lowers his blood glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks hepatic glucagon receptors to reduce glycogenolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mimics native incretins to enhance beta-cell insulin secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits somatostatin release from pancreatic delta cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Translocates GLUT4 to myocyte membranes without insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supplies the C-peptide absent from synthetic insulin preparations

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists reproduce the native incretin signal that drives insulin release after a meal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liraglutide and exenatide are GLP-1 receptor agonists used for the hyperglycemia of type 2 diabetes. They mimic the action of the native incretins, which are secreted by the gut after a meal and activate pancreatic beta cells, complementing insulin's effect to lower the serum glucose level.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These agents act on the GLP-1 receptor of the beta cell rather than antagonizing hepatic glucagon receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delta-cell somatostatin release is not the target of incretin-based therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 translocation without insulin occurs with muscle contraction during exercise, not with a GLP-1 agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C-peptide is a byproduct of proinsulin cleavage with no glucose-lowering action being replaced here.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: Delta cells are scattered throughout the islets of Langerhans and secrete growth hormone-inhibiting hormone, also known as somatostatin. Within the islet itself, this peptide most directly does which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stimulates insulin secretion from beta cells during hyperglycemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stimulates glucagon secretion from alpha cells during hypoglycemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converts proinsulin into mature insulin within beta-cell granules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promotes GLUT4 translocation in adjacent exocrine acinar cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits secretion of both insulin and glucagon by neighboring cells

explanation.summary: Islet somatostatin is a local paracrine brake on both alpha and beta cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delta cells release somatostatin into the islet interstitium, where it inhibits alpha-cell glucagon secretion and beta-cell insulin secretion alike. Somatostatin is also made in the hypothalamus, where it suppresses growth hormone and prolactin release, and in the GI tract, where it slows secretion and motility, but those are separate pools with separate roles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Somatostatin suppresses insulin release rather than stimulating it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Somatostatin inhibits alpha-cell glucagon output; hypoglycemia itself is the stimulus for glucagon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proinsulin is cleaved by enzymes inside beta-cell granules, a process unrelated to delta-cell secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT4 is expressed in skeletal and cardiac muscle and adipose tissue and is moved by insulin, not by somatostatin.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has 6 months of weight loss and watery diarrhea along with a red, blistering rash that migrates across her perineum and lower extremities. Fasting plasma glucose is 265 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor arising from pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tumor arising from pancreatic delta cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tumor arising from pancreatic alpha cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor of intestinal cells that secrete GLP-1

explanation.summary: Hyperglycemia with weight loss, diarrhea, and migratory necrolytic erythema is the classic glucagonoma picture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucagonoma is a rare tumor of pancreatic alpha cells. Unregulated glucagon drives hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, producing marked hyperglycemia, and the syndrome also features weight loss, diarrhea, and the migratory necrolytic erythema described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A beta-cell tumor hypersecretes insulin and produces hypoglycemia with confusion or seizures, not hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delta cells produce somatostatin, which is not the source of a migratory blistering rash with hyperglycemia in this lecture's framework.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction causes type 1 diabetes; it does not produce the characteristic rash and diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLP-1 is an incretin that lowers serum glucose, so excess would not cause a fasting glucose of 265 mg/dL.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A college basketball player asks about carbohydrate loading and eats a large pasta meal several hours before her game. As insulin rises in response to the absorbed glucose, the excess nutrient is deposited in which of the following forms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycogen in liver and skeletal muscle and triglyceride in adipose tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycogen in adipose tissue and triglyceride in liver and skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free amino acids in skeletal muscle and glycogen in adipose tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free fatty acids bound to albumin and glycogen in red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycogen in brain and red blood cells and triglyceride in the liver

explanation.summary: Insulin stores fuel as hepatic and muscle glycogen first and as adipose triglyceride once glycogen stores fill.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin promotes glucose storage in liver and muscle as glycogen, the primary short-term storage form. Once the liver is saturated with glycogen, additional glucose taken up by hepatocytes is converted to fatty acids, esterified into triglycerides, and packaged into VLDL; lipoprotein lipase then releases fatty acids for adipocyte uptake, where insulin-stimulated glucose becomes the glycerol backbone for stored triglyceride.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This inverts the tissues: adipose tissue stores triglyceride, while liver and muscle store glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin promotes protein synthesis rather than accumulation of free amino acids, and adipose tissue does not serve as a glycogen depot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Circulating albumin-bound fatty acids are a transport pool, not a storage form, and red blood cells do not store glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Brain and red blood cells take up glucose for immediate use through insulin-independent transporters and do not store it as glycogen.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: During an oral glucose tolerance test, glucose entering a pancreatic beta cell is metabolized by glycolysis and the intracellular ATP-to-ADP ratio rises. Which of the following events follows most directly from this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels in the beta-cell membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exocytosis of preformed insulin granules at the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Entry of glucose into the beta cell through GLUT2 transporters

choices.label: D
choices.text: Closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the beta cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hyperpolarization of the beta cell by increased potassium efflux

explanation.summary: A rising ATP-to-ADP ratio closes the beta cell's ATP-sensitive potassium channels, the step that couples metabolism to secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose enters through GLUT2 and is metabolized, generating ATP. The high ATP closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels, which depolarizes the membrane; depolarization then opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the resulting rise in intracellular calcium moves insulin granules to the membrane for exocytosis. Channel closure is the event that immediately follows the metabolic signal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium channel opening requires depolarization, which occurs only after the potassium channels have already closed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exocytosis is the final step and depends on the calcium influx that lies two steps further downstream.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose entry through GLUT2 precedes glycolysis and therefore comes before, not after, the rise in ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potassium efflux is reduced when the channels close, so the cell depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizing.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Endocrine Pancreas

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with rapid deep breathing, excessive thirst, frequent urination, and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss over 3 weeks despite eating more than usual. He is thin and appears dehydrated. Plasma glucose is 486 mg/dL, and serum and urine ketones are elevated. Which of the following additional laboratory findings would most strongly support type 1 rather than type 2 diabetes in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin A1c of 11.4%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fasting triglyceride concentration of 320 mg/dL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Undetectable serum C-peptide concentration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fasting plasma glucose of 168 mg/dL on repeat testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated fasting serum insulin concentration

explanation.summary: Low or absent C-peptide marks the absolute insulin deficiency that defines type 1 diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin during endogenous insulin synthesis and is released in equimolar amounts with insulin, making it a reliable marker of beta-cell function. In T1DM the beta cells are destroyed, so C-peptide is low or absent, whereas in T2DM it is normal or elevated. This is one of the two mechanism-establishing tests, along with islet autoantibodies, used once hyperglycemia is confirmed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated HbA1c confirms sustained hyperglycemia but is seen in both types and says nothing about the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypertriglyceridemia is a feature of metabolic syndrome and does not distinguish the two types; its absence does not exclude either.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL confirms diabetes but does not identify which type is present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A high endogenous insulin level points away from absolute deficiency and toward insulin resistance.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has lost 5 kg over the past month even though her appetite has increased and she is eating larger meals than usual. Plasma glucose is 342 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains her weight loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of insulin's brake on lipolysis and proteolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Suppression of glucagon secretion by persistent hyperglycemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Appetite suppression by circulating ketone bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced glucose uptake by brain and red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoantibody blockade of peripheral insulin receptors

explanation.summary: Insulin is the body's brake on catabolism, so its absence breaks down fat and protein despite abundant circulating glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin is the master fed signal and the primary restraint on catabolism. When it is absent, storage stops and lipolysis and protein breakdown are unleashed, so fat and lean mass are consumed for fuel. Combined with urinary calorie loss from glucosuria, this produces weight loss even when appetite is normal or increased.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucagon is not suppressed in T1DM; loss of insulin leaves glucagon unopposed, which further drives gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patients with new-onset T1DM are characteristically hungry, and polyphagia is one of the three Ps of the classic presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Brain and red blood cells take up glucose through insulin-independent transporters and continue to do so regardless of insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The autoantibodies of T1DM are markers of beta-cell destruction, not receptor blockers, and symptoms come from lack of insulin itself.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with newly diagnosed diabetes has been urinating large volumes and drinking constantly for 2 weeks. His plasma glucose is 388 mg/dL and urinalysis shows 4+ glucose with no infection. Which of the following best explains his high-volume urine output?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deficient posterior pituitary release of antidiuretic hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osmotic diuresis from glucose exceeding tubular reabsorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Renal tubular resistance to circulating antidiuretic hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased glomerular filtration rate from expanded plasma volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary loss of ketoacids obligating sodium and water excretion

explanation.summary: Polyuria in diabetes is an osmotic diuresis that begins when plasma glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorptive capacity.
explanation.whyCorrect: When plasma glucose exceeds the kidney's variable capacity to reabsorb filtered glucose, often approximated near 180 mg/dL, glucose spills into the urine and holds water in the tubular lumen. The resulting osmotic diuresis produces high-volume urination and free water loss, and the ensuing volume depletion drives compensatory thirst. This is the mechanism behind the polyuria and polydipsia of the classic presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deficient ADH release describes central diabetes insipidus, which does not produce hyperglycemia or 4+ glucosuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tubular resistance to ADH describes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, a separate cause of polyuria with normal plasma glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This patient is volume depleted from ongoing water loss, not volume expanded, and glucosuria of this magnitude is the operative problem.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ketoacid excretion is a downstream consequence of unrestrained lipolysis and is not the principal osmotic driver of the polyuria.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A pancreatic specimen from a patient who died shortly after presenting with new-onset type 1 diabetes shows dense lymphocytic infiltration of the islets with loss of beta cells. Which of the following best describes the immunologic mechanism responsible for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation within the islets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of circulating immune complexes in islet capillaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complement-mediated lysis of beta cells by anti-GAD antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell-mediated destruction by T lymphocytes and macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extracellular amyloid deposition compressing the islet cells

explanation.summary: Type 1 diabetes is a type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity in which T cells and macrophages destroy beta cells, producing insulitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: B lymphocytes present islet autoantigens to helper T cells, which release cytokines that recruit T lymphocytes and macrophages; these effector cells directly destroy the beta cells. Histologically this appears as lymphocytic infiltration, or insulitis, with progressive islet beta-cell loss. Autoantibodies such as anti-GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, and insulin autoantibodies are markers of this process rather than the primary mediators of cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is a type I hypersensitivity mechanism and does not cause insulitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune complex deposition is a type III mechanism and is not the lesion described in the islets in T1DM.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Islet autoantibodies mark the autoimmune process but are not the direct cause of beta-cell death in this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Islet amyloid deposition is a feature of type 2 diabetes and does not explain a lymphocytic infiltrate.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old nurse is evaluated for recurrent episodes of confusion and diaphoresis. During a documented episode, plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL, serum insulin is markedly elevated, and C-peptide is suppressed. Which of the following best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin-secreting pancreatic islet cell tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administration of exogenous insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surreptitious use of a sulfonylurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral insulin resistance with compensatory hypersecretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults

explanation.summary: High measured insulin with suppressed C-peptide identifies the insulin as exogenous, since injected insulin contains no C-peptide.
explanation.whyCorrect: C-peptide is co-secreted in equimolar amounts with endogenous insulin, but insulin preparations that are injected contain none. Therefore a high insulin level paired with a low C-peptide level during hypoglycemia indicates that the insulin came from outside the body. Note that this pattern identifies the source of the insulin only; it does not by itself establish a diabetes type, since anyone who injects insulin shows it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An insulinoma secretes endogenous insulin, so insulin and C-peptide would both be elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A sulfonylurea stimulates the beta cell, so endogenous secretion raises insulin and C-peptide together.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin resistance is associated with high C-peptide from compensatory endogenous secretion, and it does not cause hypoglycemia of this severity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults presents with hyperglycemia and still has measurable C-peptide early in its course.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl whose brother has type 1 diabetes is found to have two islet autoantibodies on screening. Her fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c are normal and she has no symptoms. Overt hyperglycemia in this disease typically appears only after loss of approximately what proportion of beta cells?

explanation.summary: Autoantibodies appear years before symptoms, and clinical hyperglycemia emerges only after roughly 80% of beta cells are lost.
explanation.whyCorrect: The autoimmune attack on beta cells is gradual, and autoantibodies including anti-GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, and insulin autoantibodies can be detected years to decades before any symptom. Clinical hyperglycemia emerges only once beta-cell loss exceeds roughly 80%, which is why a child can be antibody positive with normal glucose. The presence of two or more autoantibodies confers a nearly 100% risk of eventually developing insulin-requiring disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of this small a fraction leaves ample beta-cell reserve, and glucose remains normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Substantial reserve remains at this level of loss, so glucose tolerance is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Even after losing about half the beta-cell mass, remaining secretion keeps glucose in the normal range.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperglycemia appears before beta-cell destruction is complete, and residual secretion may persist around the time of diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old asymptomatic man has a fasting plasma glucose of 131 mg/dL on a screening panel drawn after an overnight fast. He has no polyuria, polydipsia, or weight loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in establishing the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Repeat the fasting glucose to confirm the abnormal result

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diagnose diabetes on this single value and begin therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measure islet autoantibodies to establish whether diabetes is present

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obtain a random plasma glucose to confirm the diagnosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defer any further testing until symptoms of hyperglycemia develop

explanation.summary: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, a diagnostic result must be confirmed by a second abnormal test.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher meets a diagnostic threshold, but in a patient without unequivocal hyperglycemia the criteria require two abnormal results, from the same or from different diagnostic tests. Repeating the test is therefore the next step before the diagnosis is made. Only classic hyperglycemic symptoms or a hyperglycemic crisis with a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher removes the need for confirmation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A single abnormal value in an asymptomatic patient does not satisfy the diagnostic criteria and should be confirmed first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoantibodies establish the mechanism once hyperglycemia is confirmed; they do not diagnose diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A random glucose is diagnostic only in a patient who has symptoms of hyperglycemia, which this man lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting for symptoms ignores an already abnormal fasting value that meets a diagnostic threshold.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with hereditary hemolytic anemia and a markedly shortened red cell lifespan reports 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and a 4 kg weight loss. Random plasma glucose is 289 mg/dL, but her HbA1c is 5.7%. Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between her symptoms and her HbA1c?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her symptoms are too recent to have raised plasma glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rapid red cell turnover lowers the measured glycated fraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anemia falsely lowers laboratory plasma glucose measurement

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbA1c reflects glucose control over the preceding 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residual C-peptide secretion normalizes long-term glycemia

explanation.summary: HbA1c can be falsely low when red cells turn over rapidly, so a normal value does not exclude diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: HbA1c is the percentage of hemoglobin that is glycated, and it reflects roughly the preceding 2 to 3 months because red cells circulate about 120 days. Conditions with rapid red cell turnover, such as hemolytic anemia, shorten the exposure time and falsely lower the measured value. A value below 6.5% therefore does not exclude diabetes, and in this symptomatic patient the random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher is diagnostic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Her plasma glucose is in fact markedly elevated at 289 mg/dL, so the premise of this explanation is wrong.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anemia does not falsely lower a plasma glucose measurement; the glucose value here is genuinely high.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbA1c integrates glycemia over roughly 2 to 3 months, not over a single day.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preserved C-peptide would not normalize an HbA1c in the face of glucose values in this range.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is ready for discharge on a physiologic outpatient regimen. Insulin aspart has been prescribed with each meal. Which of the following should be added to suppress hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin glargine once daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin lispro before bedtime snacks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin twice daily with meals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glipizide once daily before breakfast

choices.label: E
choices.text: An additional dose of aspart at bedtime

explanation.summary: The basal-bolus regimen pairs a long-acting basal insulin with rapid-acting mealtime insulin to mimic normal pancreatic secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-acting insulins such as glargine or detemir provide the basal component that suppresses hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight. Rapid-acting agents such as lispro or aspart cover the postprandial rise at meals. Combining the two is the current standard of care because it reproduces the physiologic pattern of endogenous secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lispro is a rapid-acting bolus insulin, so it covers a meal rather than providing between-meal basal coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No oral agent substitutes for insulin in T1DM, where beta-cell destruction has produced absolute deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfonylureas act by stimulating beta cells, which have been destroyed in this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adding another rapid-acting dose provides brief coverage rather than the sustained basal effect that is needed.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man with type 1 diabetes managed with an insulin pump has had three episodes in the past month of shakiness, confusion, and profuse sweating during the late afternoon, each relieved by drinking juice. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin delivery in excess of current needs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interruption of insulin delivery by the pump

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accumulation of ketone bodies from lipolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unopposed glucagon driving hepatic glucose output

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osmotic diuresis from sustained hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: Hypoglycemia from excess insulin is the most common acute complication in treated type 1 diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin therapy is a therapeutic tightrope: too little risks diabetic ketoacidosis, while too much causes hypoglycemia, which is the most common acute complication in treated T1DM. Shakiness, confusion, and diaphoresis are the classic warning symptoms that patients and caregivers are taught to recognize and treat promptly. Relief after carbohydrate intake supports hypoglycemia as the cause.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interrupted insulin delivery causes hyperglycemia and ketosis, not symptoms relieved by drinking juice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ketone accumulation produces Kussmaul respirations, nausea, and altered consciousness rather than symptoms resolving with sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Unopposed glucagon raises blood glucose, which cannot explain adrenergic symptoms that resolve with carbohydrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osmotic diuresis causes polyuria and volume loss and requires hyperglycemia, the opposite of what these episodes reflect.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 5 years ago has an HbA1c of 6.8% and no visual complaints. She has never had an eye examination since her diagnosis. Which of the following best describes when a dilated comprehensive eye examination should begin in adults with type 1 diabetes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the time of diagnosis, then every 5 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Five years after onset, then individualized intervals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ten years after disease onset, then every 2 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: At age 40, regardless of disease duration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only when visual symptoms or an abnormal HbA1c appears

explanation.summary: In adult type 1 diabetes, retinopathy screening starts 5 years after onset, with follow-up individualized thereafter.
explanation.whyCorrect: For adults with T1DM, a dilated comprehensive eye examination should begin 5 years after disease onset. Follow-up is then individualized, often annually, though intervals of 1 to 2 years may be reasonable after normal examinations with stable glycemia. Renal screening follows a parallel schedule, with urine albumin and eGFR assessed at least annually once T1DM duration reaches 5 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Screening at diagnosis is not the recommendation for T1DM, and a fixed 5-year interval is too long once screening begins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Waiting a decade delays detection well past the point at which retinopathy screening is indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening is tied to disease duration rather than to reaching a particular age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinopathy is asymptomatic in its early stages, which is precisely why systematic screening is required.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a BMI of 23 kg/m2 was diagnosed with diabetes 8 months ago and started on oral therapy. Despite adherence, his HbA1c has risen from 7.4% to 9.6% and he has lost 5 kg. Anti-GAD antibodies are positive and C-peptide is low. Which of the following best explains his course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune beta-cell failure presenting in adulthood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progressive insulin resistance from visceral adiposity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonadherence to the prescribed oral regimen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monogenic diabetes with an inherited secretory defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Falsely elevated HbA1c from delayed red cell turnover

explanation.summary: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults is autoimmune beta-cell failure presenting after childhood and often first misclassified as type 2 diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Age is a clue, not a rule, in T1DM: roughly 60% of new cases each year are diagnosed in adults, and latent autoimmune diabetes in adults describes autoimmune beta-cell failure that first appears in adulthood. These patients are often initially labeled as having T2DM and then fail oral therapy as beta-cell function declines. A lean habitus, catabolic weight loss, positive anti-GAD antibodies, and low C-peptide all identify the process as autoimmune and predict a need for insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin resistance is associated with obesity and with normal or elevated C-peptide, neither of which fits this lean, C-peptide-low patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonadherence would not explain positive islet autoantibodies or a low C-peptide level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monogenic diabetes is considered when autoantibodies are absent; here the anti-GAD antibodies are positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: His rising HbA1c is corroborated by weight loss and worsening control, so a spurious laboratory value does not explain the course.

questions.topicName: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated after routine screening shows a fasting plasma glucose of 134 mg/dL, confirmed at 140 mg/dL on repeat testing. She feels mildly tired but denies polyuria, polydipsia, or weight loss. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 with recent central weight gain, and her mother and older brother have diabetes. Which of the following additional physical examination findings would most strongly support underlying insulin resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffuse hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Symmetric, painless, diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: Velvety hyperpigmentation of the posterior neck and axillae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wide purple abdominal striae with proximal muscle weakness

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nonpitting thickening of the skin over the anterior shins

explanation.summary: Acanthosis nigricans is the classic cutaneous marker of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acanthosis nigricans is a velvety hyperpigmentation of skin folds at the neck, axillae, and groin, and it signals underlying insulin resistance. Patients often report that the discoloration persists despite vigorous cleaning. Together with central obesity, it is one of the physical findings that raises suspicion for T2D in an otherwise asymptomatic patient found on screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperpigmentation of creases and mucosa reflects excess ACTH-driven pigmentation, not the insulin-resistance phenotype described in T2D.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A diffusely enlarged thyroid points to primary thyroid disease and is not a marker of peripheral insulin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Purple striae with proximal weakness indicates cortisol excess; it is not the cutaneous sign linked to insulin resistance in this lecture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nonpitting pretibial skin thickening is a dermal finding of thyroid disease, not a sign of resistance to insulin.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 has a fasting plasma glucose of 108 mg/dL and an HbA1c of 6.0%. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated fasting insulin concentration. Which of the following best explains the combination of near-normal glucose with high circulating insulin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compensatory increase in beta-cell insulin secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased hepatic glucose output from unsuppressed gluconeogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased renal tubular reabsorption of filtered glucose

explanation.summary: In prediabetes, beta cells hypersecrete insulin to compensate for peripheral resistance, holding glucose near normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: As insulin resistance rises, pancreatic beta cells increase insulin secretion, and during this compensatory phase plasma glucose stays near-normal or only mildly elevated. This is exactly why a patient with significant insulin resistance can have a high fasting insulin with an essentially normal glucose. Glucose enters the diabetic range only when sustained demand exhausts beta-cell reserve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction lowers insulin production, which is the pattern of type 1 diabetes, not hyperinsulinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excess hepatic glucose output raises glucose but does not itself explain a high circulating insulin level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucagon excess stimulates hepatic glucose production; it does not drive beta-cell hypersecretion of insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced renal glucose reabsorption produces glycosuria and would not raise the fasting insulin level.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with obesity and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes has impaired glucose disposal on metabolic testing. Skeletal muscle, the body's major site of glucose disposal, fails to take up glucose despite adequate circulating insulin. Which of the following cellular defects best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of circulating insulin from beta-cell destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced delivery of glucose to muscle from capillary loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased adipose glucose uptake diverting substrate away from muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 to the cell surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess glycogen synthase activity trapping glucose inside myocytes

explanation.summary: Muscle insulin resistance is a failure of insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation to the membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose uptake in skeletal muscle normally depends on insulin-stimulated movement of GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface. In insulin resistance this translocation is impaired, so muscle cannot take up and use glucose as fuel even when insulin is present. Because muscle is the body's major site of glucose disposal, this defect contributes heavily to the rise in circulating glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin is normal or high in early T2D; complete insulin absence describes type 1 diabetes rather than resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lecture attributes impaired muscle glucose disposal to a transporter signaling defect, not to loss of capillary delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adipose tissue shares the same GLUT4 defect and takes up less, not more, glucose in insulin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased intracellular glucose trapping would enhance, not impair, net glucose uptake by muscle.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a fasting plasma glucose of 168 mg/dL after an overnight fast with no caloric intake. She has taken no medications and has not eaten since the previous evening. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for her fasting hyperglycemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continued hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis despite insulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued intestinal absorption of glucose from the prior meal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced glomerular filtration of glucose by the kidneys overnight

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells eliminating basal insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased skeletal muscle release of stored glucose into blood

explanation.summary: Fasting hyperglycemia in T2D reflects active hepatic glucose overproduction, not just failed uptake.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin normally suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, but with hepatic insulin resistance this suppression is blunted and the liver keeps exporting glucose. This underappreciated contribution means fasting hyperglycemia is driven by active overproduction of glucose rather than only by impaired peripheral uptake. Inappropriately elevated glucagon in T2D further stimulates this hepatic glucose output.

whyWrongByChoice.B: After an overnight fast, intestinal absorption of the prior meal is no longer a meaningful source of plasma glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Altered renal handling of glucose changes glycosuria, and it is not the mechanism the lecture assigns to fasting hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-cell autoimmunity defines type 1 diabetes; this patient's T2D involves resistance with preserved insulin secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot export stored glucose back into the circulation.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with visceral obesity and type 2 diabetes is found to have markedly elevated circulating free fatty acids. Which of the following best explains this laboratory finding and its metabolic consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced adipocyte GLUT4 function, increasing substrate available for fat storage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of adipocytes, releasing stored lipid into the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess hepatic ketone production, raising measured fatty acids in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired renal clearance of lipids, allowing fatty acids to accumulate in plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adipocyte resistance to insulin's antilipolytic effect, releasing free fatty acids

explanation.summary: Insulin-resistant adipocytes release excess free fatty acids that further worsen resistance elsewhere.
explanation.whyCorrect: In adipose tissue the same GLUT4 defect reduces glucose uptake, but more importantly the adipocyte becomes resistant to insulin's antilipolytic effect and spills free fatty acids into the circulation. That excess FFA load then worsens insulin resistance in both liver and muscle, compounding the cycle. This lipotoxic burden also contributes to the beta-cell dysfunction that follows.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipose GLUT4 function is impaired in insulin resistance, and better fat storage would lower rather than raise circulating FFAs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adipocytes are not an autoimmune target in T2D; the autoimmunity of type 1 diabetes is directed at islet cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most T2D patients retain enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis, and ketone production does not explain elevated FFAs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture attributes the FFA excess to unrestrained lipolysis in adipose tissue, not to defective clearance.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes undergoes mixed-meal testing. After the meal her plasma glucagon fails to fall and remains inappropriately elevated. Which of the following best explains this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic alpha cells with hormone leakage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired insulin-mediated paracrine suppression of pancreatic alpha cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of somatostatin-secreting delta cells from islet amyloid deposits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of skeletal muscle GLUT4 transporters to reach the membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess renal glucose loss triggering a counterregulatory hormone surge

explanation.summary: Postprandial glucagon stays high in T2D because insulin's paracrine suppression of alpha cells is impaired.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin normally suppresses glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells by a paracrine effect in the postprandial state. In T2D this suppression is impaired, so glucagon levels are inappropriately elevated after meals. The unopposed glucagon then further stimulates hepatic glucose output, compounding the hyperglycemia produced by resistance and beta-cell failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha cells are intact in T2D; the problem is failure to suppress them, not destruction with hormone release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amyloid deposition in T2D is described as a mechanism of beta-cell dysfunction, not as delta-cell loss driving glucagon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GLUT4 translocation defect explains impaired muscle glucose uptake, not the postprandial glucagon response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal glucose loss produces glycosuria and is not the described trigger for the elevated glucagon in T2D.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has a waist circumference of 110 cm, serum triglycerides of 260 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol of 52 mg/dL, blood pressure of 120/76 mm Hg, and fasting plasma glucose of 92 mg/dL. Which of the following additional findings would establish a diagnosis of metabolic syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: LDL cholesterol of 168 mg/dL

choices.label: B
choices.text: Body mass index of 31 kg/m2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Total cholesterol of 245 mg/dL

choices.label: D
choices.text: HDL cholesterol of 32 mg/dL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum uric acid of 8.4 mg/dL

explanation.summary: Metabolic syndrome requires any 3 of 5 criteria: abdominal obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL, hypertension, and fasting hyperglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient already meets two criteria, abdominal obesity by waist circumference and elevated triglycerides, while his blood pressure and fasting glucose are normal. Adding a low HDL cholesterol supplies the third of the five criteria and establishes metabolic syndrome. The syndrome is a clinical marker of the insulin resistance that underlies type 2 diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated LDL cholesterol is not among the five criteria; the lipid criteria are high triglycerides and low HDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abdominal obesity for this diagnosis is measured by waist circumference rather than BMI, which is already accounted for here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Total cholesterol is not one of the defining criteria for the syndrome regardless of its value.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperuricemia is not part of the five-criterion definition used to make this clinical diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes is brought in after 3 days of confusion during a urinary tract infection. Plasma glucose is 812 mg/dL and serum osmolality is markedly elevated, but serum ketones are only minimally positive and arterial pH is 7.36. Which of the following best explains the absence of significant ketoacidosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating islet autoantibodies neutralize the ketogenic effect of glucagon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Severe hyperglycemia directly inhibits hepatic fatty acid oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residual endogenous insulin secretion is sufficient to suppress ketogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marked hyperosmolality prevents free fatty acids from reaching the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal excretion of ketoacids fully compensates for hepatic overproduction

explanation.summary: HHS rather than DKA is the characteristic hyperglycemic crisis in T2D because residual insulin blocks ketogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 2 diabetes is most often complicated acutely by hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state rather than diabetic ketoacidosis, because most patients retain enough residual insulin secretion to suppress ketogenesis even as glucose climbs to dangerous levels. DKA can still occur in T2D under severe physiologic stress such as infection or myocardial infarction, or in very late-stage disease with beta-cell exhaustion. Here the very high glucose and osmolality with minimal ketosis fit HHS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Islet autoantibodies are markers of type 1 diabetes and are generally absent in T2D; they do not block ketone formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperglycemia itself does not inhibit hepatic fatty acid oxidation; insulin is the factor that restrains ketogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperosmolality does not prevent fatty acid delivery to the liver, and this is not the explanation for the low ketone level.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal excretion cannot offset the ketoacid production seen in true DKA; ketogenesis is suppressed at the source here.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 44-year-old asymptomatic woman with obesity is screened for diabetes at a wellness visit. Which of the following results would meet an American Diabetes Association threshold for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fasting plasma glucose of 118 mg/dL after an overnight 8-hour fast

choices.label: B
choices.text: Random plasma glucose of 172 mg/dL drawn shortly after lunch

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin A1c of 6.1% measured on a standardized assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fasting serum insulin well above the upper limit of normal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two-hour glucose of 214 mg/dL on oral glucose tolerance testing

explanation.summary: ADA thresholds are FPG at least 126 mg/dL, HbA1c at least 6.5%, 2-hour OGTT glucose at least 200 mg/dL, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: A 2-hour OGTT glucose of at least 200 mg/dL meets the ADA threshold, so 214 mg/dL qualifies for the diagnosis. Because hyperglycemia here is not unequivocal and the patient is asymptomatic, the result should be confirmed on repeat testing. The OGTT remains a valid criterion even though it is not frequently used now.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A fasting plasma glucose of 118 mg/dL is below the diagnostic threshold of 126 mg/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The random glucose criterion requires a value of at least 200 mg/dL and applies only to symptomatic patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An HbA1c of 6.1% falls below the diagnostic cutoff of 6.5% for diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An elevated fasting insulin reflects beta-cell compensation for resistance and is not a diagnostic criterion.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns for follow-up and his hemoglobin A1c is reported as 8.4%. Which of the following does this value best represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycated hemoglobin reflecting control over the past 2 to 3 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plasma glucose at the moment the blood sample was drawn in clinic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endogenous insulin secretion measured over the preceding 24 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proportion of filtered glucose that is lost in the urine daily

choices.label: E
choices.text: Beta-cell reserve remaining relative to the patient's insulin demand

explanation.summary: HbA1c reports glycated hemoglobin as a fraction of total hemoglobin and tracks control over roughly 2-3 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hemoglobin A1c test reports glycated hemoglobin as a fraction of total hemoglobin, and the value rises as average glucose levels rise. It therefore shows how well controlled blood sugar has been over approximately the past 2 to 3 months. A standardized assay is required, and a value of 6.5% or higher meets the ADA diagnostic threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A point-in-time plasma glucose is what the random or fasting glucose measures, not the A1c.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endogenous insulin secretion is assessed with insulin or C-peptide levels rather than glycated hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urinary glucose loss is not what the A1c quantifies; it measures hemoglobin glycation in the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Remaining beta-cell reserve is inferred from C-peptide and clinical course, not from the A1c value.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 has had gradually rising glucose over 8 months and now has a fasting plasma glucose of 158 mg/dL. Laboratory studies show a low C-peptide level and positive anti-GAD65 antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with early beta-cell failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young

choices.label: C
choices.text: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metabolic syndrome without overt diabetes

explanation.summary: Low C-peptide with positive islet autoantibodies indicates autoimmune diabetes, which in an adult is LADA.
explanation.whyCorrect: C-peptide is released with endogenous insulin in equal amounts, so a low level signals marked beta-cell loss rather than the preserved secretion of T2D. Islet autoantibodies such as GAD65 are present in most patients with autoimmune diabetes and are generally absent in T2D. Age alone is unreliable, since type 1 diabetes can begin in adults as latent autoimmune diabetes in adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T2D characteristically shows normal or elevated C-peptide and negative islet autoantibodies, the opposite of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MODY is a monogenic form typically seen in younger, non-obese patients and is not an autoantibody-positive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHS is an acute hyperglycemic complication, not a classification of the underlying diabetes type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metabolic syndrome is a clinical cluster of resistance criteria and does not explain autoantibody positivity with low C-peptide.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 16 years, managed with oral agents. His HbA1c has drifted upward despite adherence, and his physician now starts basal insulin. Which of the following best explains the need for insulin therapy in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of his disease into type 1 diabetes mellitus now

choices.label: B
choices.text: New autoimmune destruction of islets by anti-GAD65 antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete resolution of peripheral insulin resistance over years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive failure of beta-cell reserve relative to insulin demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of glucagon secretion from the pancreatic alpha cells

explanation.summary: Needing insulin in long-standing T2D reflects exhausted beta-cell reserve, not conversion to type 1 diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sustained demand from insulin resistance eventually exhausts beta-cell reserve through glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and possibly islet amyloid deposition. As beta-cell mass and function decline, secretion becomes inadequate relative to demand and exogenous insulin is required. The lecture stresses that this reflects advanced beta-cell failure, not a change in the type of diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T2D does not convert into T1D; the need for insulin marks advanced beta-cell reserve failure within T2D.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Islet autoantibodies are generally absent in T2D and are not the reason long-standing patients require insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin resistance persists in these patients; it does not resolve, and its resolution would reduce insulin needs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucagon in T2D is inappropriately elevated because insulin fails to suppress alpha cells, not lost.

questions.topicName: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2D)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is evaluated for hypertension that remains at 166/102 mm Hg despite three antihypertensive agents. He reports intermittent muscle cramps and fatigue but no headache or palpitations. Laboratory studies show serum potassium 2.8 mEq/L, serum bicarbonate 33 mEq/L, suppressed plasma renin activity, and an elevated plasma aldosterone concentration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primary aldosteronism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secondary aldosteronism from renal artery stenosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)

explanation.summary: Hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin, and elevated aldosterone is the classic pattern of primary aldosteronism.
explanation.whyCorrect: In primary aldosteronism the adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone autonomously, outside normal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system feedback. Sodium retention expands extracellular volume and raises blood pressure, which in turn suppresses renin release, while enhanced potassium and hydrogen ion secretion produce hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Resistant hypertension accompanied by hypokalemia and elevated bicarbonate is the clinical clue that should trigger this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Secondary aldosteronism raises aldosterone because renin is high; this patient's renin is suppressed, which excludes an upstream RAAS driver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inappropriate antidiuresis produces hypotonic hyponatremia with concentrated urine, not hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deficient vasopressin causes dilute polyuria with high serum sodium and osmolality; it does not suppress renin or elevate aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal resistance to vasopressin also causes dilute polyuria and possible hypernatremia rather than a mineralocorticoid-excess laboratory pattern.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with confirmed primary aldosteronism has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and a serum bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains this combination of laboratory findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced distal sodium delivery limits potassium secretion while filtered bicarbonate is retained

choices.label: B
choices.text: Distal sodium reabsorption makes the lumen more negative, driving potassium and acid secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aldosterone stimulates proximal tubular bicarbonate generation while trapping potassium intracellularly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane drives water and potassium into the tubular lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction reduces potassium delivery to the collecting duct

explanation.summary: Aldosterone-driven sodium reabsorption in principal cells creates a lumen-negative gradient that promotes potassium secretion, and separate stimulation of hydrogen ion secretion produces metabolic alkalosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aldosterone increases epithelial sodium channel and Na+/K+ ATPase activity in collecting duct principal cells. As sodium leaves the lumen, the lumen becomes relatively more negative, and that electrical gradient favors potassium secretion into the urine, causing hypokalemia. Aldosterone also promotes hydrogen ion secretion, largely through intercalated cells, so urinary acid loss raises serum bicarbonate and produces metabolic alkalosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distal sodium delivery and reabsorption are increased, not reduced, and it is that reabsorption that drives potassium loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aldosterone acts on the late distal nephron and collecting duct rather than generating bicarbonate proximally, and potassium is lost in the urine rather than trapped in cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aquaporin-2 insertion is the vasopressin pathway for water permeability and does not move potassium into the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin and angiotensin II are suppressed in primary aldosteronism, and vasoconstriction is not the mechanism of the potassium and bicarbonate changes.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has blood pressure of 158/96 mm Hg despite maximally dosed therapy with three agents including a thiazide. Repeated measurements show serum potassium between 3.0 and 3.3 mEq/L and serum bicarbonate of 31 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adrenal venous sampling of both adrenal veins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma aldosterone and renin with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water deprivation testing with serial urine osmolality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Desmopressin administration with measurement of urine osmolality

explanation.summary: Suspected primary aldosteronism is screened with aldosterone, renin, and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio before any imaging or localization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis should prompt screening for mineralocorticoid excess. In primary aldosteronism renin is suppressed while aldosterone is inappropriately high, giving an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Only after a positive screen, usually with confirmatory suppression testing, does evaluation move on to determining whether the excess is unilateral or bilateral.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal computed tomography shows anatomy but not hormone secretion, so it cannot establish that aldosterone excess is present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adrenal venous sampling is a subtype-localization study performed after the diagnosis has been screened and confirmed, not a first test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Water deprivation testing is used in the evaluation of polyuria and free-water disorders, not in mineralocorticoid excess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Desmopressin testing distinguishes central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and has no role in evaluating hypertension with hypokalemia.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has a positive aldosterone-to-renin ratio and confirmatory testing showing that aldosterone fails to suppress normally. Computed tomography demonstrates a 1.2-cm right adrenal nodule and mild thickening of the left adrenal gland. Which of the following studies best determines whether the aldosterone excess is unilateral or bilateral?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal venous sampling of both adrenal veins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeat computed tomography with thinner adrenal sections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat measurement of the aldosterone-to-renin ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat aldosterone suppression testing after a salt load

choices.label: E
choices.text: Water deprivation testing with serial urine osmolality

explanation.summary: Computed tomography shows structure, whereas adrenal venous sampling shows which gland is actually secreting.
explanation.whyCorrect: An adrenal nodule on imaging does not prove that the nodule is the source of aldosterone, and bilateral hyperplasia can look deceptively asymmetric. Adrenal venous sampling measures aldosterone output from each adrenal vein and therefore determines whether excess secretion is coming from one gland or both. That distinction matters because unilateral disease may be treated surgically while bilateral disease is managed medically.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Better anatomic resolution still cannot tell which gland is hypersecreting, since imaging does not measure hormone output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The screening ratio has already been positive; repeating it adds nothing about laterality.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Suppression testing confirms autonomy of secretion, a step already completed here, and does not localize the source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Water deprivation testing evaluates polyuria and free-water handling and has no role in aldosterone subtyping.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man with confirmed primary aldosteronism undergoes adrenal venous sampling, which demonstrates excess aldosterone secretion from both adrenal glands consistent with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unilateral adrenalectomy of the larger adrenal gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desmopressin given intranasally each evening

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free-water restriction to less than one liter daily

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tolvaptan, a selective vasopressin receptor antagonist

explanation.summary: Bilateral aldosterone excess is treated medically by blocking aldosterone at the kidney with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of primary aldosteronism follows the mechanism: either remove the autonomous source or block the aldosterone signal at its renal receptor. When adrenal venous sampling shows that both glands are oversecreting, no single gland can be removed, so mineralocorticoid receptor blockade is used to prevent the sodium retention, potassium wasting, and hydrogen ion loss driven by aldosterone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenalectomy is reserved for confirmed unilateral disease; removing one gland leaves the other hypersecreting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desmopressin replaces absent vasopressin in central diabetes insipidus and does nothing for aldosterone excess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluid restriction addresses free-water retention such as in inappropriate antidiuresis, not autonomous aldosterone secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasopressin receptor antagonists are used in selected hyponatremic states and do not block the mineralocorticoid receptor.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension has an abdominal bruit and a serum creatinine that rose after starting an ACE inhibitor. Laboratory studies show elevated plasma renin activity and an elevated plasma aldosterone concentration. Which of the following best interprets this hormonal pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primary aldosteronism from an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary aldosteronism from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secondary aldosteronism from upstream activation of the RAAS

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arginine vasopressin resistance affecting collecting duct principal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion from an occult malignancy

explanation.summary: High aldosterone with high renin means the adrenal gland is responding appropriately to upstream renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Renin is the discriminating measurement. Reduced renal perfusion, as in renal artery stenosis, drives juxtaglomerular renin release, which generates angiotensin II and in turn stimulates the zona glomerulosa. Aldosterone is therefore high because renin is high, the defining feature of secondary aldosteronism, in contrast to primary disease where aldosterone is high despite suppressed renin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aldosterone-producing adenoma secretes autonomously and suppresses renin; elevated renin argues against it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilateral hyperplasia is also autonomous and likewise produces high aldosterone with suppressed, not elevated, renin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal resistance to vasopressin causes dilute polyuria with a tendency to hypernatremia and does not raise renin and aldosterone together.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inappropriate antidiuresis is a free-water disorder producing hypotonic hyponatremia and is not defined by renin and aldosterone levels.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: Water permeability of the collecting duct is regulated by hormonal insertion of channels into the apical membrane of principal cells. Which of the following best describes the pathway that directly increases collecting duct water permeability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldosterone acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor to increase ENaC activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Angiotensin II acting on vascular receptors to raise systemic arterial tone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aldosterone acting on intercalated cells to increase hydrogen ion secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vasopressin acting on V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renin acting on juxtaglomerular cells to increase Na+/K+ ATPase activity
