explanation.summary: Vasopressin is the free-water signal: V2 receptor activation inserts aquaporin-2 channels that make the collecting duct water permeable.
explanation.whyCorrect: When plasma osmolality rises, hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger posterior pituitary release of vasopressin. In collecting duct principal cells, vasopressin binds V2 receptors and activates a cyclic AMP and protein kinase A pathway that inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. Water then enters the cell and exits basolaterally through aquaporin-3 and aquaporin-4, producing more water reabsorption, lower urine volume, and more concentrated urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epithelial sodium channel activity governs sodium reabsorption and salt-volume balance rather than water permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure through vasoconstriction and adrenal stimulation, not by altering collecting duct water channels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrogen ion secretion by intercalated cells affects acid-base balance and contributes to alkalosis in aldosterone excess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells to generate angiotensin II; it does not act on the collecting duct.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman develops intense thirst and passes 8 L of dilute urine daily beginning two days after transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary macroadenoma. Serum sodium is 151 mEq/L, serum osmolality is high, and urine osmolality is low. After administration of desmopressin, her urine osmolality rises substantially. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin to replace the deficient hormonal signal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist to block renal sodium retention

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free-water restriction to reduce ongoing water retention

choices.label: D
choices.text: Discontinuation of any agent causing renal resistance to vasopressin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Behavioral reduction of excessive voluntary water intake

explanation.summary: Postoperative dilute polyuria with hypernatremia that concentrates the urine after desmopressin is vasopressin deficiency, treated by replacing the hormone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pituitary surgery is a classic cause of arginine vasopressin deficiency, traditionally called central diabetes insipidus. Without vasopressin, aquaporin-2 is not inserted into collecting duct principal cells, so free water is lost as large volumes of dilute urine and serum sodium and osmolality rise. The rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin proves the kidney can still respond, so treatment simply supplies the missing signal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the mineralocorticoid receptor targets aldosterone excess, a salt-volume disorder, and would not correct free-water loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Restricting water in a hypernatremic patient losing free water would worsen the deficit; fluid restriction is used for water excess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drug-induced renal resistance underlies nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, but here the kidney responded normally to desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excess intake defines primary polydipsia, which lowers rather than raises serum sodium and osmolality.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman treated with lithium for eight years reports passing large volumes of urine and drinking constantly. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L with high serum osmolality, and urine osmolality is low. After desmopressin is given, urine osmolality remains essentially unchanged. Which of the following best explains her findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Posterior pituitary release of vasopressin has become inadequate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collecting duct principal cells fail to respond to circulating vasopressin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excessive water intake has appropriately suppressed vasopressin release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vasopressin effect persists despite a low plasma osmolality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autonomous aldosterone secretion is driving an osmotic diuresis

explanation.summary: Dilute polyuria with hypernatremia and no response to desmopressin indicates vasopressin resistance, or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
explanation.whyCorrect: In arginine vasopressin resistance the hormone is present but the kidney cannot execute the message, typically because of lithium therapy, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, chronic kidney disease, or inherited defects of the V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 pathway. Free water is therefore lost as dilute urine, raising serum sodium and osmolality. Because the defect is renal, giving exogenous desmopressin produces little or no rise in urine osmolality, which is what separates it from vasopressin deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deficient hormone release would produce the same polyuria, but urine osmolality would rise after desmopressin because the kidney can respond.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Suppression of vasopressin by excess intake lowers serum sodium and osmolality rather than producing hypernatremia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Persistent antidiuretic effect causes hypotonic hyponatremia with concentrated urine, the opposite of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aldosterone excess is recognized by hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, not by dilute polyuria.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history and a newly identified lung mass is admitted with confusion. He is normotensive and euvolemic on examination, and urine output has been normal. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L and serum osmolality is low. Which of the following urine findings is most consistent with his diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High urine volume with maximally dilute urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: High urine volume with inappropriately concentrated urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low urine volume with a urine osmolality below serum osmolality

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal urine volume with maximally dilute urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal urine volume with inappropriately concentrated urine

explanation.summary: Inappropriate antidiuresis produces hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and low or normal urine volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: Small cell lung carcinoma is a classic cause of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, in which vasopressin effect persists even though plasma osmolality is low. Continued aquaporin-2 insertion means the kidney keeps reabsorbing free water, so urine remains concentrated when it should be maximally dilute. It is not a polyuria disorder, so urine volume is low or normal rather than high.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dilute polyuria is the pattern of diabetes insipidus or primary polydipsia, both of which occur with high or low-normal serum sodium rather than concentrated urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Large-volume urine is not a feature of inappropriate antidiuresis, in which water is retained rather than lost.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A urine osmolality below serum osmolality in this hypotonic patient would indicate suppressed vasopressin effect, not persistent antidiuresis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maximally dilute urine would be the appropriate renal response to hyponatremia and would argue against inappropriate antidiuresis.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia drinks 9 to 10 L of water daily and reports frequent urination of large volumes of clear urine. Serum sodium is 133 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and urine osmolality is low. Which of the following best explains her findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water intake exceeding need, appropriately suppressing vasopressin release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inadequate posterior pituitary release of vasopressin after hypothalamic injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collecting duct resistance to an intact circulating vasopressin signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent vasopressin effect despite low measured plasma osmolality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autonomous adrenal aldosterone secretion with renal potassium wasting

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia is excess water intake that lowers plasma osmolality and appropriately switches off vasopressin, giving dilute polyuria with low-normal sodium.
explanation.whyCorrect: In primary polydipsia the endocrine axis is intact and behaving correctly. Excess intake lowers plasma osmolality, hypothalamic osmoreceptors reduce vasopressin release, aquaporin-2 is withdrawn, and the kidney excretes the surplus water as large volumes of dilute urine. Serum sodium and osmolality are therefore low or low-normal, and during water deprivation urine begins to concentrate as endogenous vasopressin rises.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Deficient hormone release causes free-water loss with high or high-normal serum sodium and high serum osmolality, not hypotonic values.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal resistance likewise produces free-water loss with a tendency to hypernatremia rather than a low serum osmolality.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Persistent antidiuretic effect would produce concentrated urine in the face of hyponatremia, whereas her urine is dilute.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aldosterone excess is a salt-volume disorder recognized by hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with biochemically confirmed primary aldosteronism has blood pressure of 162/98 mm Hg, serum potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and serum bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. His serum sodium is 142 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains why his serum sodium is not markedly elevated despite ongoing renal sodium retention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldosterone increases sodium excretion once extracellular volume has expanded

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldosterone regulates potassium and hydrogen ions without affecting sodium transport

choices.label: C
choices.text: Suppressed renin prevents any sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retained sodium is accompanied by water, so the sodium concentration changes little

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coexisting vasopressin deficiency causes free-water loss that masks sodium retention

explanation.summary: Serum sodium is a concentration, so sodium retention with proportional water retention expands volume without producing severe hypernatremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum sodium reflects the relationship between body sodium and body water, not total body sodium alone. In primary aldosteronism the retained sodium expands extracellular fluid volume and raises blood pressure, while water intake, vasopressin regulation, and renal escape mechanisms keep the sodium concentration near normal. This is why the high-yield pattern is hypertension with low renin, high aldosterone, low potassium, and metabolic alkalosis rather than high sodium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption rather than excretion; the excess secretion here is autonomous and persistent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone acts on sodium transport directly by increasing epithelial sodium channel and Na+/K+ ATPase activity in principal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renin suppression is a consequence of volume expansion and does not switch off aldosterone-driven distal sodium reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no indication of deficient vasopressin here, and free-water loss would raise rather than normalize serum sodium.

questions.topicName: Endocrine Messages to the Kidney: Hyperaldosteronism, ADH Disorders, and Diabetes Insipidus

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is seen for routine follow-up. He has been taking metformin for 6 years with an HbA1c of 6.9%. Repeat laboratory studies now show a serum creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL with an estimated GFR of 24 mL/min/1.73 m2. His physician stops the metformin. Which of the following adverse effects is the reason this drug is contraindicated in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lactic acidosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fasting hypoglycemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral edema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute pancreatitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genital candidiasis

explanation.summary: Metformin is contraindicated when a condition predisposes to lactic acidosis, including CKD with GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metformin's rare but potentially fatal adverse effect is lactic acidosis. It is therefore contraindicated in conditions that predispose to it: chronic kidney disease with markedly reduced GFR (<30 mL/min/1.73 m2), severe congestive heart failure, and progressive liver disease. For the same reason it is temporarily held around iodinated contrast studies and restarted only after renal function is confirmed stable.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Metformin carries a low risk of hypoglycemia, which is one of its advantages over the insulin secretagogues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluid retention and peripheral edema are the hallmark problems of thiazolidinediones acting through PPAR-gamma, not of metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute pancreatitis is a recognized adverse effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists and, rarely, of DPP-4 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genital candidiasis follows the glycosuria produced by SGLT2 inhibitors, not by metformin.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus returns for follow-up with an HbA1c of 8.5% despite adherence to metformin. His history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, hypertension, and obesity. His physician plans to add a second glucose-lowering agent. Which of the following agents is most likely to worsen his cardiac condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empagliflozin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Semaglutide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pioglitazone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sitagliptin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acarbose

explanation.summary: Thiazolidinediones cause sodium and fluid retention through PPAR-gamma and should generally be avoided in heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pioglitazone activates PPAR-gamma, which increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting tubules. The resulting fluid retention produces peripheral edema and can precipitate or worsen heart failure, so patients with heart failure should generally avoid thiazolidinediones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiac events in patients with cardiovascular disease and are an attractive second agent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce cardiac events in coronary artery disease and promote weight loss without fluid retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral and generally well tolerated; only saxagliptin has been linked to heart failure hospitalization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors act in the gut lumen; their main problem is flatulence, not fluid retention.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus takes insulin glargine each evening and an injection before each meal. She realizes at the table that she forgot her pre-lunch dose and wants the preparation that will cover this meal with the fastest onset of action. Which of the following insulin preparations is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin aspart

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regular insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: NPH insulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin detemir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin degludec

explanation.summary: Rapid-acting insulin analogs have the fastest onset and are the mealtime component of a basal-bolus regimen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rapid-acting analogs such as insulin aspart have the quickest onset of any preparation and are given up to 15 minutes before a meal to mimic the prandial insulin peak. They are also the insulins used in insulin pumps.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Regular insulin is short-acting with a slower onset and should be given 30 to 60 minutes before a meal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NPH is intermediate-acting, combined with protamine and zinc to delay absorption, and is used for basal coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Detemir is a long-acting basal insulin and does not provide prandial coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Degludec forms multihexamer depots and has the longest duration of the daily basal insulins.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with vomiting and Kussmaul respirations. Serum glucose is 512 mg/dL, bicarbonate is 8 mEq/L, and serum ketones are strongly positive. After fluid resuscitation is begun, the team wants to start a continuous intravenous insulin infusion. Which of the following preparations can be administered by this route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NPH insulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regular insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin glargine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin degludec

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin icodec

explanation.summary: Short-acting regular insulin is the only formulation that can be given intravenously and is the agent used in acute hyperglycemic crises.
explanation.whyCorrect: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the only insulin formulation that can be administered intravenously, which is why it is used in diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, and severe hyperkalemia. Given intravenously it acts immediately rather than over the 30 to 60 minutes required subcutaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NPH is given subcutaneously only, never intravenously, and is not appropriate for rapid glucose lowering in DKA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glargine precipitates in subcutaneous tissue to release insulin slowly and is a basal agent only.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Degludec relies on subcutaneous multihexamer formation for its ultra-long action and is not an intravenous drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Icodec is an ultra-long-acting basal insulin dosed subcutaneously once weekly through albumin binding.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and prior myocardial infarction is started on empagliflozin in addition to metformin. Her fasting glucose falls and urinalysis at the next visit shows 3+ glucose with no ketones or leukocyte esterase. Which of the following best describes the mechanism responsible for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activation of nuclear PPAR-gamma receptors in adipocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the enzyme that degrades endogenous GLP-1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of brush-border enzymes that digest carbohydrates

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors block the proximal tubule transporter that reclaims filtered glucose, so glucose is lost in the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose is normally reabsorbed by SGLT2 transporters in the proximal tubule and appears in urine only with marked hyperglycemia. Gliflozins block that transporter, so serum glucose falls independently of insulin levels or beta-cell function and glycosuria appears even at ordinary glucose levels. The accompanying osmotic diuresis also produces weight loss.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Channel closure describes sulfonylureas and meglitinides, which raise insulin secretion rather than urinary glucose losses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PPAR-gamma activation is the thiazolidinedione mechanism, which improves insulin sensitivity without causing glycosuria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking DPP-4 raises endogenous incretin levels and enhances glucose-dependent insulin release; urine glucose does not rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors blunt postprandial glucose absorption in the gut and do not cause renal glucose wasting.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought in after a fall at home. She is confused, diaphoretic, and tachycardic; fingerstick glucose is 44 mg/dL. Her only diabetes medication is glipizide, started 2 weeks ago. Which of the following best describes how this drug produces her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closes beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, triggering insulin exocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds a Gs-coupled receptor that raises beta-cell cAMP during meals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevents degradation of endogenous incretin hormones after eating

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increases GLUT-4 translocation and suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Delays gastric emptying and suppresses postprandial glucagon release

explanation.summary: Sulfonylureas force insulin release by closing beta-cell K-ATP channels, so hypoglycemia occurs regardless of the ambient glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sulfonylureas close ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells, causing depolarization, voltage-gated calcium influx, and exocytosis of insulin granules. Because this release is not glucose-dependent, the resulting insulin surge can drive glucose down far enough to cause confusion, dizziness, falls, and coma, and excretion is further reduced in older patients with chronic kidney disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The Gs-coupled GLP-1 receptor is the target of incretin mimetics, which rarely cause hypoglycemia because their effect is glucose-dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking incretin degradation is the DPP-4 inhibitor mechanism; these agents do not typically cause hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT-4 translocation with reduced gluconeogenesis is metformin's mechanism, and metformin carries a low hypoglycemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delayed gastric emptying with glucagon suppression describes amylin analogs and GLP-1 agonists, not sulfonylureas.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus reports burning and stinging at the injection site each evening when he takes his basal insulin. His glucose tracings show a flat, essentially peakless effect over the following 24 hours. Which of the following properties best explains both findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A low isoelectric point causing precipitation in subcutaneous tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complexation with protamine and zinc that delays absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of multihexamers that create a slow-release depot

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strong albumin binding that stretches release over about a week

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fusion to an IgG Fc domain that prolongs the circulating half-life

explanation.summary: Insulin glargine's low isoelectric point makes it precipitate at the injection site, producing a peakless profile and injection-site stinging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glargine has a lower isoelectric point than human insulin, so it precipitates once injected into the neutral pH of subcutaneous tissue. The precipitate dissolves slowly, giving the flat, peakless basal profile, and the same acidic formulation and precipitation account for the burning or stinging sensation patients describe.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Protamine and zinc complexation describes NPH, an intermediate-acting insulin that does have a peak and is not associated with this sting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multihexamer formation is how degludec achieves the longest duration among daily basal insulins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin binding with release over roughly a week describes insulin icodec, a once-weekly basal insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An insulin linked to an IgG Fc domain describes insulin efsitora alfa, another once-weekly basal preparation.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus on a basal-bolus regimen still has glucose readings of 260 to 300 mg/dL two hours after meals despite appropriate bolus dosing. Her physician adds pramlintide, injected with insulin at each meal. Which of the following best describes how this drug improves her postprandial readings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It replaces a beta-cell peptide that slows gastric emptying and lowers glucagon

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks intestinal enzymes that release glucose from complex carbohydrates

choices.label: C
choices.text: It closes potassium channels so residual beta cells release stored insulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It blocks renal glucose reabsorption so the meal load is excreted in urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: It activates nuclear receptors that shift muscle toward glucose utilization

explanation.summary: Pramlintide is an analog of amylin, the peptide cosecreted with insulin, and replaces it in patients whose islets are destroyed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amylin is a small peptide cosecreted with insulin by pancreatic beta cells that reduces glucagon secretion, slows gastric emptying, and increases satiety. Islet destruction in type 1 diabetes leaves patients deficient in both insulin and amylin, so pramlintide is injected with insulin at meals as an adjunct for inadequate postprandial control in insulin-treated patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking brush-border carbohydrate digestion is the acarbose and miglitol mechanism, and those drugs are not amylin replacements.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Closing beta-cell potassium channels requires functioning beta cells, which this patient has lost to autoimmune destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal glucose excretion is the SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism and is not how a mealtime amylin analog works.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nuclear receptor activation describes thiazolidinediones, which address insulin resistance rather than postprandial peaks.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and moderate hyperglycemia is started on a new oral agent taken with the first bite of each meal. Two weeks later he reports bloating and considerable flatulence, and his physician reassures him that gradual dose escalation usually relieves this. Which of the following mechanisms explains both the glucose lowering and the symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delayed digestion of complex carbohydrates at the intestinal brush border

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced intestinal glucose absorption with increased GLUT-4 translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slowed gastric emptying through replacement of a beta-cell peptide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased incretin levels through inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase-4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osmotic diuresis from blocked glucose reabsorption in the nephron

explanation.summary: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors blunt postprandial glucose by delaying carbohydrate digestion, and undigested carbohydrate causes gas and bloating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-glucosidase enzymes at the intestinal brush border break complex carbohydrates into absorbable glucose. Acarbose and miglitol inhibit them, delaying digestion and lowering postprandial glucose. The carbohydrate that escapes digestion is fermented downstream, producing the bloating and flatulence, which can be minimized by increasing the dose gradually.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced gut absorption plus GLUT-4 translocation is metformin, whose GI complaints are nausea, diarrhea, and metallic taste.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Replacement of amylin describes pramlintide, an injectable adjunct whose main adverse effects are nausea and vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DPP-4 inhibitors are oral but typically cause nasopharyngitis and headache rather than flatulence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osmotic diuresis from blocked renal reabsorption describes SGLT2 inhibitors, which cause dehydration and urogenital infections.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease has an HbA1c of 9.4% with persistent polyuria despite maximal metformin. Her BMI is 38 kg/m2 and her estimated GFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. She is willing to use an injectable medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to add?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Semaglutide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dapagliflozin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glyburide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rosiglitazone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repaglinide

explanation.summary: GLP-1 agonists are the preferred add-on for an obese patient with cardiovascular disease and HbA1c above 9%, particularly when renal function limits SGLT2 inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists are especially effective in patients with persistent symptoms or HbA1c above 9% despite metformin. They reduce cardiac events in coronary artery disease and promote weight loss through delayed gastric emptying and satiety, and they rarely cause hypoglycemia. Their subcutaneous dosing, which can last up to a week, is acceptable to this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT2 inhibitors work poorly once eGFR falls below 45 mL/min/1.73 m2 because their action depends on filtered glucose delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia, and their excretion is reduced in chronic kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiazolidinediones promote weight gain through adipocyte proliferation and fluid retention, the opposite of what she needs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Meglitinides act like sulfonylureas, causing hypoglycemia and weight gain, and require frequent dosing before each meal.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Diabetes with Glucose-Lowering Agents

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus taking metformin and canagliflozin presents with 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after a low-carbohydrate diet and a viral illness. Serum glucose is 188 mg/dL, bicarbonate is 11 mEq/L, anion gap is 22 mEq/L, and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated. Lactate is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug-induced acute pancreatitis

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate ketoacidosis with only modestly elevated glucose because they lower serum glucose independently of insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gliflozins lower serum glucose by dumping it in the urine, independently of insulin levels or beta-cell function. In patients with low insulin secretion, especially under a stressor such as illness or carbohydrate restriction, ketogenesis proceeds while the urinary glucose loss keeps the serum glucose near normal, producing a high-anion-gap ketoacidosis at a glucose level that would otherwise be reassuring.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is defined by extreme hyperglycemia with minimal ketosis, not a glucose of 188 mg/dL with heavy ketonemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis would show an elevated lactate, and her lactate is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: She is not taking insulin, and her glucose is elevated rather than below 70 mg/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatitis is a GLP-1 agonist and DPP-4 inhibitor adverse effect and would not produce ketonemia with an anion-gap acidosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus had two hypoglycemic episodes on glipizide, both occurring hours after meals were skipped. His physician stops the glipizide and starts repaglinide, dosed before each meal. Which of the following properties of the new drug best accounts for its lower risk of hypoglycemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its shorter half-life, which requires more frequent dosing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its action on the GLP-1 receptor rather than the potassium channel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its glucose-dependent stimulation of insulin secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its predominant effect on hepatic rather than pancreatic tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its clearance by the kidney rather than by the liver

explanation.summary: Hypoglycemia risk among glucose-lowering drugs tracks with half-life, so short-acting meglitinides are safer than sulfonylureas but must be dosed more often.
explanation.whyCorrect: The risk of hypoglycemia from glucose-lowering drugs is directly related to the drug's half-life. Meglitinides such as repaglinide share the sulfonylurea mechanism but have a rapid onset and a shorter duration of action, so the insulin surge does not persist into a missed meal. The trade-off is that they must be dosed more frequently, before each meal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Meglitinides do not act at the GLP-1 receptor; their mechanism overlaps that of sulfonylureas, which is why the two are not combined.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose-dependent insulin release describes the incretin-based agents; meglitinides stimulate secretion regardless of glucose level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meglitinides act on pancreatic beta cells; reducing hepatic glucose output is a feature of metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal clearance would prolong, not shorten, drug exposure in an older patient and would raise hypoglycemia risk.
